queue.recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands, on the small patch of grass at the corner of Sudurgata and Vonarstraeti, hard against the parking area near City Hall.
queue.story: In 1918, the year the Act of Union made Iceland a sovereign state in union with Denmark, a sycamore maple went into the ground at the corner of Suðurgata and Vonarstræti, on a small patch of grass squeezed against what would later become a parking area. It grew alongside the birth of modern Icelandic statehood, was named the country's Tree of the Year in 1994, and by every recent assessment is still, in the Icelandic forestry society's own phrase, healthy as a horse, crown maintained, foliage vigorous, standing its ground on a corner most passers by would assume was chosen for parking rather than for a tree planted before the country existed in its current form. Sycamore maple is not native
queue.name: The City Hall Maple
queue.worth: the tree already has one: ship this only if it is better

queue.recognise: You can recognise it in winter, when it stands bare among the cemetery's evergreens: a conifer that drops its needles. It grows in Holavallagardur, along the gravel paths between the headstones.
queue.story: European larch does not grow wild anywhere near Iceland, and conifers in general struggle against the country's wind and thin soil more than almost any other kind of tree, which is part of why Iceland's forestry society singled one out in 2011 growing inside Hólavallagarður, Reykjavik's oldest surviving cemetery. Consecrated in 1838 and still the resting place of many of the country's most significant historical figures, the cemetery has become, almost by accident, one of the most heavily wooded plots of ground in the capital, its narrow gravel paths winding between headstones and trees rather than through open lawn the way most cemeteries are laid out. queue.name: The Larch of Hólavallagarður

queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the one old tree in the little park, put in the ground in 1884 at the corner of Adalstraeti and Kirkjustraeti and reckoned the oldest planted tree in the country.
queue.story: Reykjavik's oldest tree stands on ground that was the city's main burial ground for roughly six centuries, from a church first recorded around 1200 until the last graves stopped in 1839. In 1883 the Danish health director Georg Schierbeck took over the disused churchyard for horticultural experiments, planting vegetables, grain, shrubs and trees to test what could actually grow in Iceland's climate, and the following summer he put a Swedish whitebeam in the ground at the corner of Aðalstræti and Kirkjustræti.
